Earthdial

Earth as it is right now, seen from any viewpoint you choose; by default, from far above the North Pole. Every clock shown is official local time. Based on xkcd #1335, “Now.”

      Choosing a viewpoint

      Each view is set by the Sun: from the North Pole the Sun is straight up the page, and the other views are turned from that one. Live, the view keeps up with the Sun, so Earth turns beneath it; when you press Play the view freezes to the ground at that moment and the Sun travels around Earth instead. From the North Pole the rim is the equator and only the northern hemisphere shows; from the South Pole Earth turns clockwise. Orbital north and south look down the normal to Earth's orbital plane from either side, where day and night meet along a straight line. From the Sun you see the whole day side. From the Moon you see the face of Earth turned toward it right now; the lit fraction is Earth's phase as seen from the Moon, the complement of the Moon's phase seen from here. Drag to turn the view anywhere in between. Set Sun to Stays still to keep the Sun in place during playback too. See through Earth draws the far hemisphere as if the planet were glass: from the South Pole you look up through Antarctica at the northern hemisphere, mirror-reversed, with its own day and night.

      The shape of the night

      Day and night meet along a great circle facing the Sun. From over the North Pole it projects to half an ellipse with semi-axes 1 and |sin δ|, where δ is the Sun's declination. At the equinoxes it is a straight diameter. In northern winter it bows toward the Sun and the pole sits in darkness; in summer it bows the other way. Pick Loop → Year to watch it swing: that loop steps one whole day at a time at a fixed clock time, so the continents hold still while the seasons change.

      The Sun's size

      The Sun is drawn far larger than its true size, as a disc seven times Earth's width whose near edge sits just past the edge of the frame. Seen from near Earth the real Sun spans only about 0.53° (0.524° to 0.542° over the year), which at true scale would be a speck that could not plausibly light a whole hemisphere. Its size keeps the picture consistent: a Sun this much larger than Earth makes Earth's shadow a converging cone that still reaches past the Moon, as the real one does, and from the Moon the Sun lies within about 10° of the direction seen from Earth, so the two are lit alike. The lighting itself uses the real Sun's direction, as parallel rays. Its surface imitates the Sun in extreme ultraviolet (as NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory sees it at 304 Å): an orange mottled network with bright active regions, dark filaments, and a ragged edge with prominences.

      Official time

      The thin borders on land outline the real time zones as currently defined, daylight saving included, and pointing anywhere gives the official time there. The ring shows standard time for the 24 nominal zones centered on multiples of 15°, so a place on daylight saving reads one hour ahead of the ring. Each hour mark sits where that hour has just begun, so the ring turns with the Sun: still when the Sun is still, smoothly when it moves. The UTC mark is the prime meridian. When you set a clock city, the ring switches to that city's official time, daylight saving included: the amber mark on its meridian is the hour hand, and the UTC mark moves to where the ring reads UTC. The outer strip is an ordinary minute dial, 0 at the top and one turn an hour; its white marker shows the minutes of the same clock. Each marker can be turned off under Overlays, and turning off the minute marker removes its strip. Under Clock hands you can draw hands instead (Meridian, Skeleton or Bezel; press H to cycle them): the hour hand lies along the clock city's meridian, through its star, and reads its official hour on the ring, and the minute hand is an ordinary one. Above 1 h/s the minute hand is left out, since it would spin several turns a second.

      Inspired by xkcd #1335, “Now” by Randall Munroe (CC BY-NC 2.5); Earthdial is an independent homage and does not reuse its artwork. Surface imagery: NASA Blue Marble (day) and Black Marble (night lights), public domain. Time-zone boundaries: timezone-boundary-builder 2025b, © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL. City list: city-timezones (MIT), from Natural Earth populated places. Official times come from your browser's time-zone database. Solar position from the standard low-precision almanac formulas, good to about 0.01°.
